title: From Vision to Prediction: A Multimodal-AI Pipeline to Generate Perceptual Attributes for Price Prediction
affiliations: Audencia Business School and Audencia Business School

detail.title: From Vision to Prediction: A Multimodal-AI Pipeline to Generate Perceptual Attributes for Price Prediction
detail.abstract: We examine whether multimodal artificial intelligence, particularly its vision capabilities, can enhance price prediction by expanding the information set typically used by researchers and practitioners. We develop a generic pipeline to derive perceptual attributes from photographs of tangible goods that are likely to affect buyers' willingness to pay. We enforce a three-stage approach in which an AI generates: (1) an economically grounded taxonomy of attributes; (2) a dictionary of ordinal values for each attribute with explicit evaluation rules; and (3) attribute grades based on a good's photographs. We apply our pipeline to the context of housing prices, using 1,142 residential house transactions. We show that the AI-generated perceptual attributes contain substantial incremental information beyond the standard structured attributes available from online listings. Relative to machine-learning house price models based solely on conventional attributes, incorporating perceptual attributes leads to a consistent and significant improvement in predictive performance.

title: Sunk-cost, Responsibility, and Belief

detail.title: Sunk-cost, Responsibility, and Belief
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the roles of responsibility, ex-post rationalization, and belief in sunk-cost decisions through a two-stage investment task in a laboratory setting. The experiment reveals that participants exhibit a robust pro-rata fallacy (reverse sunk-cost effect): Participants are less likely to make additional investments in the presence of exogenous sunk costs. This fallacy is absent when participants are not responsible for their initial investment decisions. Ex-post rationalization does not affect the magnitude of sunk-cost bias, and sunk costs do not distort participants' beliefs about future project success.

detail.abstract: Heterogeneous returns from contributions to a public good create a normative conflict between equality and efficiency. In a laboratory experiment, we proposed an indicative menu of contribution principles including one featuring a decentralized redistribution mechanism ensuring earnings equality in exchange for fully efficient contributions. Although a majority of individuals, when in the position of an impartial observer, considered this principle to be the most appropriate and expected others to agree, they failed to act on it. Designating a leader who endorsed this principle and made non-binding recommendations enabled a majority of groups to adopt it successfully. This resulted in full contributions and earnings equalization through redistribution from advantaged to disadvantaged members, effectively resolving the conflict.

detail.abstract: The Doctrine of Force Multiplication Without Formation (DFM): Artificial Intelligence, Market Competition, and the Educational Substitution Prohibition constitutes the final and integrative work in The Governance Boundaries Canon: Foundational Doctrines for Artificial Systems, Human Judgment, and Lawful Authority. The Canon comprises four interlocking doctrines developed to preserve the constitutional preconditions of lawful authority under conditions of artificial acceleration: The Artificial Conscious Agency Doctrine (ACAD): A Constitutional, International, and Moral Framework for Synthetic Intelligence in the Post-Semiconductor Era; The Doctrine of Moral Closure in Artificial Systems: The Continuity Paradox; The Continuity vs. Conscience Doctrine (CVC): The Mappability Boundary in Artificial Systems and Human Rights; and, finally, the present doctrine. Together, these works articulate a coherent legal architecture for governing artificial systems without surrendering human judgment, moral responsibility, or constitutional legitimacy. Where the prior doctrines address agency drift, rights drift, and institutional reflex under artificial continuity pressures, DFM identifies and governs a distinct and under-theorized failure mode: judgment atrophy induced by force multiplication without corresponding human formation. Artificial intelligence dramatically multiplies speed, scale, and apparent reasoning capacity, while market competition predictably incentivizes institutions to substitute system-generated outputs for slow, burden-bearing human judgment formation—particularly in educational and professional domains. This substitution produces immediate gains in efficiency and productivity while silently eroding the human capacities that law presupposes but does not itself generate. DFM introduces a novel constitutional risk vector—the Epistemic Displacement Risk—defined as the structural relocation of judgment-bearing authority away from accountable human actors and into non-contestable systems through reliance rather than formal delegation. Unlike traditional delegation or automation concerns, epistemic displacement occurs without statute, vote, or explicit authorization, and often in the absence of error, bias, or bad faith. Its harm is prospective and structural: due process, contestability, and lawful governance degrade not because procedures fail, but because the human capacity to exercise judgment within those procedures erodes over time. DFM further demonstrates that epistemic displacement produces a corresponding macroeconomic externality—Epistemic-Economic Contagion Risk—through which the erosion of judgment formation within one jurisdiction propagates wage stagnation, credential dilution, institutional brittleness, and governance fragility across borders via globally integrated labor and capital markets. In this way, what begins as a localized substitution of formation for output scales into a systemic stability risk, mispricing judgment at the national level and transmitting institutional vulnerability through international economic systems. Drawing on constitutional doctrine, non-delegation principles, due process jurisprudence, and institutional design, DFM argues that education functions as pre-political infrastructure and that educational substitution constitutes an unlawful delegation of epistemic authority. The doctrine establishes a formal Assistance vs. Substitution test to distinguish permissible uses of artificial intelligence from constitutionally impermissible reliance, and articulates justiciable injuries and limiting principles to ensure judicial manageability. The central maxim of the doctrine is simple and durable: Force may be multiplied by machines. Judgment must not be. By naming, defining, and governing epistemic displacement before reliance hardens into necessity, DFM completes the Governance Boundaries Canon and provides courts, legislators, educators, and institutions with a principled framework for preserving lawful authority in an era of accelerating artificial capability. Finally, DFM enters into the public doctrinal record as formal constructive notice that the structural preconditions for a new class of global governance risk have now been identified with sufficient clarity to permit preventive coordination. The risks articulated herein are non-kinetic, slow-moving, and prospective, yet materially destabilizing to lawful authority, economic equilibrium, and institutional continuity if left unaddressed.

title:
It's About Time (Series):
 A Simple Correction For Difference-in-Differences Estimators
affiliations: Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) and Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)

detail.title:
It's About Time (Series):
 A Simple Correction For Difference-in-Differences Estimators
detail.abstract: This paper reconsiders the difference-in-differences (DiD) research design for panel data, particularly when serial correlation stems from first-order model misspecification (i.e., dependence in yt rather than exclusively in ϵt). When time-series issues like this are overlooked, the traditional parallel trends assumption is insufficient. In fact, for most panel applications (T > 2 periods), DiD designs will misidentify and inflate a time-invariant treatment effect. To correct this, we show that DiD assumptions should be modified for dynamic panels and how explicitly accounting for temporal dependence in the design can recover the true, dynamically-robust effect. We evaluate a simple modification to DiD designs through Monte Carlo simulations and then explore its implications with empirical examples. Two examples leverage a policy shock used in recent literature to reevaluate the impact of household credit constraints on outcomes like state-level GDP growth and labor market participation. When we implement the proposed modification, which can be as simple as incorporating a lagged outcome and group interaction into a DiD model, the results illustrate a reduction in bias predicted by theory, yielding a more generalizable estimator for most applications. Finally, we find synthetic DiD and synthetic control methods do not remedy this particular issue, as similar modifications (e.g., pre-whitening) are needed to address temporal dependence in the outcome.

title: Loss, Leisure, and Liquor: Intoxicant Consumption During Climate Distress
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management Kashipur

detail.title: Loss, Leisure, and Liquor: Intoxicant Consumption During Climate Distress
detail.abstract: This study investigates how rainfall shocks influence household intoxicant expenditure, highlighting behavioral responses to climatic stress among agricultural households in India. Using district-level panel data from the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) for 2014-2019, combined with rainfall deviations from long-period averages, the analysis estimates fixed-effects models across household types defined by irrigation access, occupation, gender, and education. The results reveal that rainfall shortfalls significantly increase intoxicant expenditure among agricultural households, particularly in male-majority and less-educated groups, suggesting that idle time and coping behavior drive consumption during adverse climatic periods. Further analysis incorporating industrial intensity from the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) 2021 shows that households in low-intensity regions, where informal employment opportunities are limited, display stronger post-monsoon increases in intoxicant spending. These findings underscore the behavioral dimension of climate vulnerability, where employment scarcity and household composition mediate responses to environmental shocks. The study argues that rural non-farm employment and micro-enterprise development can play a stabilizing role, reducing both economic and psychological costs of climatic adversity. By integrating behavioral responses into the discourse on climate adaptation, the paper provides new insights for designing holistic rural resilience policies.

title: Managing Skills and Signals: Firm Training with Career-Concerned Workers
affiliations: Charles III University of Madrid and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Managing Skills and Signals: Firm Training with Career-Concerned Workers
detail.abstract: We study how firms design training content to manage the skill distribution of careerconcerned workers. Core training builds common skills, leveling the playing field for promotions, whereas idiosyncratic training (e.g., mentorship) builds unique skills that improve the signaling value of promotions. We show that firms optimally bias the mix toward core training to attract workers and boost overall performance, despite dampening effort. Unlike the existing work, firms over-certify training to amplify career concerns and may sponsor general (transferable) training in competitive labor markets. We also analyze how promotional pay gaps, asymmetric information about performance, and cohort size affect training design.

title: Structural Economic Change and Poverty Reduction: An Analysis of Sectoral Composition in Sudan
affiliations: University of Khartoum and University of Khartoum

detail.title: Structural Economic Change and Poverty Reduction: An Analysis of Sectoral Composition in Sudan
detail.abstract: This paper examines how structural economic change has influenced poverty reduction in Sudan over 1970-2022, with a particular focus on the role of sectoral composition in a fragile and conflict-affected context. The study's objective is to assess how value-added growth in agriculture, industry, and services affects poverty outcomes, measured by the headcount ratio, poverty gap, and severity index. Methodologically, the analysis constructs annual monetary poverty indices using the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) approach, based on a lognormal distribution derived from per capita consumption and Gini coefficients, and then estimates an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to capture both short-and long-run effects of sectoral value-added growth and key macroeconomic and demographic variables, including education, exports, inflation, population, credit access, and GDP growth. The results show that growth in agriculture and industry significantly reduces poverty in the long run, whereas the services sector exerts a weak, statistically insignificant effect. Education, access to credit, and higher inflation are associated with lower poverty levels, while population growth increases poverty, and export expansion is linked to higher poverty, reflecting the enclave nature of Sudan's extractive export sectors. Overall, the findings underscore that inclusive structural transformation-centered on revitalizing agriculture, fostering industrial development, and reorienting services-along with complementary policies in human capital, finance, and macroeconomic management, is essential for sustainable poverty reduction in Sudan. The study thus provides new empirical evidence to inform policymakers in Sudan and other conflict-affected low-income economies undergoing economic transition.

title: Integration of the US Goods Market, 2001-2015
affiliations: Sovcombank Technologies LLC and Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) - Siberian Division

detail.title: Integration of the US Goods Market, 2001-2015
detail.abstract: A spatially dispersed market for a tradable good is deemed integrated if there are no barriers to trade between its spatial segments (except for geographical barriers, namely distances between the segments). However, perfectly integrated markets are not a common case; real markets deviate to some extent from this ideal state. Therefore, estimating a degree of integration is more helpful then an answer of the type "all or nothing" (whether the market is integrated or not integrated). In an integrated market, price for a good is determined in the national market as a whole, not depending on demand in its spatial segments. Hence, a dependence of local price on local demand (controlling for transportation costs) indicates a deviation from perfect integration, and its "strength" can measure the degree of market integration. Based on this idea, we estimate the annual integration degrees of the US market for an aggregated good (grocery basket) over 15 years, 2001-2015. The spatial segments are cities; our sample covers 66 cities from 39 states of the US. The results suggest that the US market is not perfectly integrated; however, the integration degree of the US market is fairly stable over time. We also compare results for the US with results of a similar study for Russia. With a reservation that the empirical material is not fully comparable, we can conclude that the US market is integrated more strongly than the Russian market and that the integration degree in Russia is more volatile.

title: Wavelet Decomposition of Coffee Price Dynamics - The Role of Temperature Shocks

detail.title: Wavelet Decomposition of Coffee Price Dynamics - The Role of Temperature Shocks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest -- either personal or financial

detail.abstract: Climate change has increased the frequency and intensity of temperature anomalies, raising concerns about their implications for agricultural commodity markets. Considerable evidence is now emerging about the increasing instability in commodity output caused by weather anomalies and subsequent emergence of risk premia embedded in price. Whereas most papers look at average effects, this paper makes use of a procedure based on a wavelet-domain regression framework to disentangle the impact of weather at the short-, medium-, and long-run time horizons for coffee futures, and relates each to a non-linear temperature threshold analysis in Brazil. The paper finds significant shock-like responses to extreme cold (below 10 • C) and extreme heat (above 38 • C) at short horizons, consistent with arabica coffee plant physiology. In contrast, temperatures between 30 • C-and 36 • C are found to have a significant dampening response on price. Moreover, earlier periods exhibit persistent medium-and long-run price components consistent with embedded weather-related risk premia, whereas such persistence largely disappears in more recent decades, suggesting a shift toward faster incorporation of temperature information.

detail.title:
Secret Agents: 
Hidden Governance of Autonomous Artificial Intelligence

declarations.funderStatement: This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. DRL-2418715.

detail.abstract: This Article examines how the historical arc of autonomous software agents, beginning with ancient Greek automatons and culminating in modern large language models, can guide the governance of artificial intelligence in contemporary society. It explores decentralization, emergent behavior, potential for surprise, and assumptions of beneficence as cornerstones of effective regulatory strategies. The discussion highlights that modern principles of AI governance may not fully capture these underappreciated dimensions, particularly as large language model agents evolve beyond simple task execution to serve as orchestrators of problem-solving in multiple fields. The text proposes a recalibration of legal structures, urging policymakers and scholars to look to the past for insights on how best to manage and channel the power of increasingly independent AI agents.

title: Antitrust for Digital Sustainability: Revitalizing the Consumer Welfare Standard through Dynamic Efficiency
affiliations: Kean University College of Business and Public Management

detail.title: Antitrust for Digital Sustainability: Revitalizing the Consumer Welfare Standard through Dynamic Efficiency
detail.abstract: Antitrust law, grounded in price theory, static efficiency, and a narrowly framed consumer welfare standard, increasingly struggles to address the complexities of the digital economy. Frameworks focused on short-term price and output effects are ill-suited to the structural challenges of platform ecosystems, data-driven markets, and rapid technological change. This Article calls for a recalibration that redefines consumer welfare through dynamic efficiency and digital sustainability. Dynamic efficiency emphasizes long-term innovation, technological progress, and systemic resilience, complementing traditional competition models. Drawing on theories of commons, anticommons, and semicommons, the Article shows how control over digital resources can foster or obstruct innovation and societal welfare. Antitrust law must therefore secure fair access to such resources, encouraging innovation while preventing monopolization and excessive fragmentation. This reconceptualization shifts core concepts like market power and market definition away from price manipulation toward a firm’s capacity to drive innovation and maintain open ecosystems. To operationalize the framework, the Article introduces two novel analytic tools: the Sustainable Dynamic Efficiency Function and the Sustainability-Conscious Hypothetical Monopolist Test. Together, they measure the systemic effects of market conduct on innovation, ecosystem openness, and long-term resilience, positioning a reformed consumer welfare standard as a compass for competition policy in the digital age.

title: Tensor-Train Approximation for High-Dimensional Economic Models
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Tensor-Train Approximation for High-Dimensional Economic Models

declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge financial support from the ERC project SOLG for Policy (101042908).

detail.abstract: We introduce a scalable and broadly applicable method to compute accurate global solutions of high-dimensional dynamic stochastic models. Our approach leverages the tensor train format for function approximation, exploiting latent low-rank structures commonly present in economic models. While able to capture complex nonlinearities, the number of parameters of the tensor train approximation (TTA) grows only linearly in dimensions, significantly mitigating the curse of dimensionality. We show that TTA can be integrated naturally into standard iterative solution schemes, can capture irregularly shaped ergodic sets, is compatible with the endogenous grid method, makes quasi-analytical computation of expectations possible, and enables spectral solutions of continuous-time models, all in high dimensions. We illustrate the scalability of TTA by solving international real business cycle models of increasing dimension at only moderately increasing compute time without deteriorating accuracy. We demonstrate the versatility of TTA by solving heterogeneous agent models with large aggregate shocks. To approximate the wealth distribution efficiently, we introduce a moment-selection procedure that identifies the most informative moments from simulated data. In a model with wealth-tax shocks, the use of the first nine such moments as inputs to TTA reduces approximation errors by one order of magnitude relative to using only mean wealth.

title: Algorithmic Constitutionalism - Normative Principles for the Constitution of the Future: Fourth-Generation Digital Rights

detail.title: Algorithmic Constitutionalism - Normative Principles for the Constitution of the Future: Fourth-Generation Digital Rights
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a disruptive legal framework titled "Algorithmic Constitutionalism," designed to address the unprecedented challenges posed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in the displacement of power toward computational architectures. The author argues that classical constitutionalism is currently in a state of  "chronological lag," unable to constrain a power that operates through code rather than traditional coercion.

The proposal, drawing from interdisciplinary insights, evolves beyond reactive regulations such as GDPR to addresses existential risks such as misalignment, automation bias, algorithmic feudalism, and plutocratic capture, while harnessing opportunities for abundance and human emancipation. Key chapters explore transhumanism, the transition of state power from coercion to computational design, polycentric global governance, blockchain-based institutional experimentation, and Universal Basic Income (UBI) as an enforceable algorithmic right.

The core contribution is a Decalogue of guiding principles —such as the supremacy of human agency, non-delegation of responsibility, reversibility, traceability, structural precaution, citizen control, constitutionalization by design, power differentiation, oracle auditing, and the abundance dividend—designed as fourth-generation digital rights to protect individual autonomy in an AGI-dominated era. Emphasizing "limit before trust to ensure progress”, bridging current ethical gaps and inspiring future legislative developments in a post-scarcity world.

title: Rohingya Refugee Camps and Land Cover Change in Bangladesh
affiliations: University of Victoria - Economics

detail.title: Rohingya Refugee Camps and Land Cover Change in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: How does the rapid establishment of a large-scale refugee camp affect competition for land and, consequently, local land cover? I examine this question in Bangladesh using high-resolution Dynamic World data (2016-2023) on Cox Bazar, a district hosting the largest refugee camp in the world. The analysis focuses on areas within 0-5 km of camp boundaries, using propensity score matching to define counterfactuals and a difference-indifferences event study framework to estimate impacts. The 2017 Rohingya refugee influx and related camp expansions reduced forest cover by 4.6 percentage points by 2019, but forests partially recovered in subsequent years. Settlement cover grew steadily, reaching 3.7 points in 2022. Results are robust across multiple specifications. Heterogeneity analysis shows that effects are strongest near the Kutupalong expansion site. Early forest losses were likely driven by biofuel extraction, while recoveries may reflect LPG cookstove programs, fencing, or both. Increases in nighttime lights indicate that settlement expansion reflects local economic growth following camp establishment.

title: Time Cost of Digital Privacy Protection and Data-Driven Innovation
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Time Cost of Digital Privacy Protection and Data-Driven Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the time cost of digital privacy protection as a proxy for the instrumental value of digital privacy and analyzes consumption-data provision and data-driven innovation in a simple Schumpeterian endogenous growth model. A higher marginal time cost of privacy protection discourages data provision, raises the cost of data-driven innovation, and reduces the long-run growth rate. When this marginal time cost is above (below) a threshold value, the market equilibrium exhibits socially excessive (insufficient) innovation, due to an intertemporal business-stealing effect. The threshold depends on the innovation step size, monopoly markups in product markets, and the data intensity of R&D. We characterize the policy instruments required to restore the social optimum. We further examine how technological and regulatory improvements affect the marginal time cost through consumers’ digital-literacy input and the intermediary’s data-security input, and assess the resulting implications for innovation and long-run growth via the data-cost channel.

title: From Physical to Online: Examining the Impact of a Sudden Shift in Business Opinion Survey Data Collection Mode in Zambia During COVID-19
affiliations: Bank of Zambia, Bank of Zambia and Bank of Zambia

detail.title: From Physical to Online: Examining the Impact of a Sudden Shift in Business Opinion Survey Data Collection Mode in Zambia During COVID-19
detail.abstract: Online surveys are an alternative to traditional in-person data collection. However, abrupt transitions between modes may have unintended consequences. This study examines the impact of a sudden shift from in-person to online survey administration in Zambia prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a panel of 1,719 firm responses from five rounds of in-person business opinion surveys (2019–early 2020) and five subsequent rounds conducted online, we assess how this mode change affected response rates and data quality. We find that the shift led to a sharp decline in response rates, particularly among rural firms and sectors with limited digital capacity. However, data quality, measured by item nonresponse, improved significantly under the online mode. These findings highlight the trade-offs involved in survey mode transitions in developing country contexts. While online platforms present important opportunities for cost-effective data collection and improved quality, their effectiveness may be hindered by gaps in digital infrastructure and low levels of digital literacy.

As we navigate the "Decade of Action," it has become evident that the linear pursuit of individual Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is insufficient to address the systemic complexity of the planetary crisis. The operationalization of SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals is not merely a supportive mechanism but the central nervous system of the entire agenda. This report provides an exhaustive, "360-degree" analysis of the implementation mechanisms, institutional coordinates, and leadership frameworks necessary to bridge the gap between national ambition and global execution. Drawing upon the "Six SDG Transformations" framework, this document maps the global constellation of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) hubs—referred to herein as "Global Coordinates"—that serve as the operational engines for these transformations. These coordinates are not abstract concepts; they are physical and institutional anchors located in specific cities and regions, from the financial districts of Dublin and London to the agricultural research centers of Texcoco and Hyderabad. title: Beyond Homogeneous Production Functions
affiliations: Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) - Siberian Division

detail.title: Beyond Homogeneous Production Functions
detail.abstract: Standard production functions, being homogeneous, have unchanging returns to scale. Therefore, it remains unclear to students where the U-shape average-cost curves come from. This article considers non-homogeneous production functions that have variable returns to scale and can produce such curves, providing a specific example. The article also discusses the link between economies/diseconomies of scale and market structures, showing that economies of scale are incompatible with perfect competition. They are peculiar to monopolies and oligopolies, whereas in a perfectly competitive market there are no economies of scale, diseconomies of scale being a quite normal phenomenon.

title: Shadows Vs. Spotlights: The Battle for Transparency in ADR
affiliations: Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha (GGSIP) University

detail.title: Shadows Vs. Spotlights: The Battle for Transparency in ADR
detail.abstract: Arbitration and mediation are often chosen for their privacy, yet contemporary trends and public interest increasingly demand openness. The inherent tension between transparency and confidentiality is central to the evolution of arbitration and mediation. This paper examines the legal foundations, practical challenges, and contemporary debates surrounding transparency and confidentiality in dispute resolution. Through comparative analysis and examination of recent developments, this paper argues that while confidentiality remains essential to the efficacy of alternative dispute resolution, selective transparency mechanisms are necessary to ensure accountability and public trust, particularly in disputes involving state entities or matters of significant public concern.

title:
Purpose-Anchored, Bidirectional Organizational Governance
A Governance Framework for Boards, CEOs, and Capacity-Building Systems

detail.title:
Purpose-Anchored, Bidirectional Organizational Governance
A Governance Framework for Boards, CEOs, and Capacity-Building Systems
detail.abstract: Organizational failures are most often attributed to poor execution, leadership shortcomings, or insufficient resources. In practice, the dominant root cause is governance failure-specifically, the erosion of purpose clarity, accountability discipline, and resistance to predictable human dysfunction. As organizations increasingly deploy artificial intelligence and other capacitybuilding systems, these weaknesses are amplified rather than corrected. This paper presents a purpose-anchored, bidirectional organizational governance framework that establishes organizational governance as the parent system within which all capacity-human and artificial-is delegated. The framework centers the Board-CEO relationship as the operational core of governance, from which culture, discipline, drift resistance, and corruption risk emerge. Governance is treated as bidirectional cognition: execution proceeds forward, while governance works backward from purpose to define success parameters, forbidden outcomes, and escalation thresholds. The paper establishes accountability as feedback rather than punishment, and recognizes the emotional pain that often accompanies accountability as a frequent-but necessary-teacher in human systems. Respect is framed as inseparable from accountability, protecting value creators while requiring corrective action when negative value is introduced. Artificial intelligence governance is positioned as an applied subset and stress-test of organizational governance, illustrating how capacity-building systems remove friction from whatever governance already permits-good or bad. The framework applies across corporate, nonprofit, charitable, and governmental organizations and provides boards and CEOs with a disciplined, reality-based approach to governing under complexity, incentives, and power.

title: Toward a Multistakeholder Governance of the Agentic Internet

detail.title: Toward a Multistakeholder Governance of the Agentic Internet
detail.abstract:
Autonomous AI agents, systems capable of planning, executing, and adapting tasks, are moving from prototypes to operational actors across the global economy. From copilots and trading bots to healthcare and logistics tools, they are multiplying fast, with projections surpassing one billion active agents by 2028 . Managing this scale demands governance suited to high-velocity, machine-to-machine environments.
Yet no shared infrastructure exists to register, verify, or hold these agents accountable. Without reliable provenance or identity, society cannot determine which agents participated in a transaction or under what guarantees. As they begin to communicate through protocols such as Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A), Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), this lack of verifiable records introduces systemic opacity that erodes safety and trust.
This white paper proposes a registry framework for AI agents, inspired by the Domain Name System (DNS) and guided by transparency, subsidiarity, and multistakeholder governance. Its layered design includes:
● Autonomy Passport: a standardized metadata record capturing each agent’s capabilities, provenance, and oversight protocols.
● Root Registry: issues unique AgentIDs and baseline policy standards.
● Registrars: provide registration, verification, and compliance-as-a-service tools.
The framework would interoperate with emerging standards and align with global policy instruments. It creates capacity to:
● Prevent misuse of unverified agents.
● Maintain oversight for critical decisions.
● Provide verifiable provenance and auditability across ecosystems.
This proposal is not a limitation on innovation but an enabler of trust, a public good forming part of the foundational governance layer of the Agentic Internet.

Sextortion scams are serious, manipulative crimes that use threats and coercion to provoke intense fear and shame, often pushing victims to the brink of desperation and, in some cases, resulting in suicide.

title: A KPI-Governed Architecture for Integrated Civilizational Renewal (ICRA): From Theological Convergence to Measurable Unity (MCPI)
affiliations: University of Religions and Denominations, University of Religions and Denominations, Tehran-North Branch, Islamic Azad University, University of Religions and Denominations and University of Religions and Denominations

detail.title: A KPI-Governed Architecture for Integrated Civilizational Renewal (ICRA): From Theological Convergence to Measurable Unity (MCPI)
detail.abstract: This article introduces the Integrated Civilizational Renewal Architecture (ICRA) and its measurement core, the Multi-Convergence Performance Index (MCPI), a composite index for assessing unity across layered domains of rapprochement (taqrīb). Powered by the DDRNIC data engine (110 validated KPIs), MCPI integrates four convergence clusters Foundations (L1), Capability (L2), Impact (L3), and Stewardship (L4) and is gated by Consent & Privacy Compliance (CPC) and a Data Quality Index (DQI) to ensure ethical and reliable reporting. Methodologically, we employ a design-science, mixed-methods approach with an explanatorysequential sequence: KPI dictionary construction and validation; surveys and document/communiqué analytics using AI-driven NLP; social network analysis for dialogue structure; and quasi-experimental designs (A/B, DiD, ITS) to attribute effects. Findings show that Foundations (L1) doctrinal coherence and a shared governance vocabulary are necessary conditions for gains in L2-L4. Dialogue Intensity and cross-axis network centrality emerge as leading indicators of cooperation. Interventions such as co-teaching of adab, family media-literacy, and digitization of waqf processes yield the most consistent, causally verified uplifts. Theoretically, the study advances a KPI-governed, gate-constrained scorecard that translates maqāṣid and adab al-ikhtilāf from principles into auditable control. Practically, it offers a portable operating system-KPI cards, common data model, CPC/DQI gates, and quarterly release cadence-enabling ministries, universities, waqf/zakat bodies, and civil society to scale unity programs with transparency and reproducibility.

title: End-to-End Swin Transformer for Predicting Remaining Useful Life of Rolling Bearings
affiliations: Hanyang University, Hanyang University, Hanyang University and Hanyang University

detail.title: End-to-End Swin Transformer for Predicting Remaining Useful Life of Rolling Bearings
detail.abstract: Accurate prediction of remaining useful life (RUL) of rolling bearings is crucial for ensuring the reliability and safety of rotating machinery systems. Traditional methods generally rely on manual feature extraction and lack the sensitivity to early-stage failures due to nonlinear degradation characteristics inherent in rolling bearings. This paper proposes a RUL prediction method using the new virtual health indicator (VHI) construction scheme by leveraging an end-to-end model based on a swin transformer encoder. The proposed approach automatically extracts VHIs from generalized spectral kurtosis of vibration signals without manual feature engineering or experiments requiring large amounts of real operational data. By incorporating the properties of both monotonicity and smoothness of signals into a gross loss function, the model explicitly captures degradation progression of rolling bearings in VHIs. The loss function is designed to reduce the variance in modeling the swin transformer network and enhance both generalization performance and interpretability for degradation features. To address the challenge of limited real-world data available, we fine-tune the VHI generation model using simulation data of bearing vibration derived from a physics-based model. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments conducted on real-world rolling bearing data sets, comparing its performance against feature-fusion and traditional health indicator based models. Analytical results show that the proposed method provides better performance in RUL prediction, particularly in nonlinear dynamic scenarios with sparse experimental data.

title: Carbon Emissions Reporting, Investment Incentives and Efficiency
affiliations: University of Zurich - Managerial Accounting and University of Graz

detail.title: Carbon Emissions Reporting, Investment Incentives and Efficiency
detail.abstract: We examine how mandatory reporting of carbon emissions affects a manager's capital allocation between brown and green investments. The manager seeks to maximize the stock price of a firm whose shareholders partially internalize emission costs. With financial reporting alone, the manager underinvests in green technology. With additional emissions reporting, the manager invests more in green technology if the market penalizes reported emissions. Moderate penalties increase efficiency. Strong penalties can result in excessive green investment, which reduces shareholder value and social surplus. If the market instead rewards emissions, underinvestment in green technology prevails. We analyze how the precision and granularity of the firm's accounting reports, the green investment type, and the manager's risk aversion affect capital allocation. We identify conditions for improving investment efficiency. Our study informs regulators about possible unintended consequences of mandatory carbon reporting and provides novel predictions for empirical research on the real effects of carbon reporting.

detail.abstract: Islamic finance has long been presented as an ethical alternative to conventional finance; however, its practical implementation has remained constrained by institutional dependence on interest-based financial architecture and manual Shariah supervision. The emergence of financial technology introduces a fundamentally different possibility: the encoding of Islamic legal and ethical constraints directly into financial systems. This paper argues that Islamic Fintech represents not an incremental innovation but a structural transformation, whereby Shariah principles are enforced at the level of financial infrastructure rather than through post hoc compliance mechanisms. By examining the convergence of Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh al-muʿāmalāt) with blockchain, smart contracts, and artificial intelligence, the paper demonstrates how Islamic Fintech can reconfigure global finance toward transparency, risk-sharing, and real economic linkage. Particular attention is given to the implications of this transformation for Muslim youth and communities, positioning Islamic Fintech as both a technological and civilizational project.

title: Cyborg Orchestration in LLM Council-Double Delphi: Protocolizing the AI Round for Ill-Structured Decisions
affiliations: State University of New York - Empire State University

detail.title: Cyborg Orchestration in LLM Council-Double Delphi: Protocolizing the AI Round for Ill-Structured Decisions
detail.abstract: Ill-structured institutional decisions, characterized by contested definitions, multiple stakeholders, incomplete data, and the absence of a definitive stopping rule, necessitate disciplined problem-structuring prior to making legitimate choices. Foundational research on illstructured and "wicked" problems highlights the co-evolution of problem formulation and solution, with solutions being evaluated as better or worse rather than true or false. The Delphi method continues to be a widely employed protocol for aggregating expert judgment under conditions of uncertainty, emphasizing iteration, controlled feedback, and structured aggregation. There is increasing focus on transparent reporting of consensus rules and stopping criteria. This working paper specifies a replicable a protocol for Phase One (the AI Round) of an LLM Council-Double Delphi methodology, building upon previous Phase-One demonstration efforts in faculty workload policy modeling (Chukhlomin, 2025). The protocol conceptualizes an LLM Council as an efficient, preliminary "expert panel" responsible for generating a structured problem map, options set, assumption register, and evidence pointers, all of which are explicitly designed for validation and adjudication by a subsequent human Delphi panel. The paper introduces the concept of Cyborg Orchestration: a human-led procedure aimed at aligning the participating models' understanding of the decision context, enforcing schema-based comparability across model outputs, and producing an auditable synthesis of convergence and divergence that serves as the agenda for human expert review. This approach is situated within (i) traditional Delphi and Double Delphi practices, (ii) problem-structuring and decision science for ill-structured problems, and (iii) emerging multi-model "council" and multi-agent orchestration frameworks.

title: PINE: Physics-Informed Neural Enhancement for Underwater Video via Implicit Representation
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University, Sun Yat-sen University and Sun Yat-sen University

detail.title: PINE: Physics-Informed Neural Enhancement for Underwater Video via Implicit Representation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (52371358 and42227901), Innovation Group Project of Southern arine Science and Engineering GuangdongLaboratory (Zhuhai)(311020011), Key-Area Research and Development Program of GuangdongProvince (2020B1111010004), National Key Research and Development Plan (2021YFC2800700)the Special project for marine economy development of Guangdong Province (GDNRC [2022]31)and (GDNRC [2021] 45).

detail.abstract: Underwater video enhancement remains challenging due to spatially varying optical properties and resolution-dependent processing in existing methods. While deep unfolding networks and physics-guided approaches have advanced the field, most operate on discrete pixel grids with fixed resolution requirements. We present PINE (Physics-Informed Neural Enhancement), which models underwater image restoration as the estimation of a continuous physical parameter field using coordinate-based implicit neural representations. PINE employs a dual-pathway encoder combining Fourier positional encoding with hierarchical image features, feeding into an implicit MLP that predicts transmission, attenuation coefficients, and background light at arbitrary spatial coordinates. The framework adopts a simplified image formation model where transmission $t(x,y)$ is predicted directly, while wavelength-dependent attenuation coefficients $\beta_c(x,y)$ serve as auxiliary regularization targets satisfying the oceanographic ordering $\beta_r \geq \beta_g \geq \beta_b$ for typical ocean waters. This formulation enables resolution-independent processing, from training patches to native 4K inference, without requiring retraining. On the UVEB benchmark, PINE achieves 30.28~dB PSNR under standardized $256 \times 256$ evaluation and 29.22~dB at native resolution with only 1.07M parameters. Ablation studies demonstrate that physics regularization is crucial for preventing parameter field collapse, with its removal resulting in a 5.57 dB degradation in PSNR. Edge deployment on Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo-8L NPU achieves real-time performance (9.4~FPS at QHD). While PINE processes frames independently without explicit temporal modeling, the coordinate-based representation provides a foundation for future spatiotemporal extensions. Code and models are available at \url{https://github.com/Jinxinshao/PINE}.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates production functions for U.S. manufacturing using a balanced panel of 598 NAICS industries covering 2007–2022. Using harmonized Census microdata deflated to 2007 dollars, we compare a two-way fixed-effects Cobb–Douglas specification with its flexible Translog extension under identical econometric conditions. Elasticities are precisely estimated: capital elasticity is small but positive (≈0.11) and labor elasticity is substantially larger (≈0.82), implying decreasing returns to scale within industries (sum ≈0.92). The Translog’s curvature and interaction terms are statistically insignificant, and its predictive performance is virtually identical to the Cobb–Douglas model across all in-sample metrics, retransformed-level fit, and 5 fold industry-level cross-validation (RMSE ≈ $12–13B; R² ≈ 0.997). Both models closely track aggregate manufacturing dynamics through the Great Recession, the post-2010 recovery, and the COVID-19 shock, but understate cross-industry dispersion during crisis years. Results indicate that a parsimonious Cobb–Douglas function is sufficient for sector-level analysis, while crisis period heterogeneity requires industry-specific modeling. This paper is an independent research project completed during secondary education.

title: Extending Aumann's Agreement Theorem to Heterogeneous Intentionality: When Rational Agents Can Agree to Disagree

detail.title: Extending Aumann's Agreement Theorem to Heterogeneous Intentionality: When Rational Agents Can Agree to Disagree

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. No financial relationships or competing interests influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study analyzed publicly available legal documents and constitutional provisions; no human subjects were involved.

detail.abstract: Aumann's (1976) "Agreeing to Disagree" theorem states that rational agents with common priors cannot hold different posterior beliefs if those posteriors become common knowledge. This foundational result underwrites game theory, mechanism design, and information economics. I argue Aumann's theorem fails when agents operate at different intentionality levels. Common knowledge requires Level 3 intentionality: agents must model others' beliefs about their own beliefs recursively ("I know you know I know"). Level 1 agents, including corporations and algorithms, lack this recursive modeling capacity. They process information but cannot achieve common knowledge with Level 3 agents. The impossibility result yields three corollaries. First, coordination failures persist even with complete information, because common knowledge of intended play cannot be achieved. Second, no-trade theorems fail, enabling Level 1 agents to exploit Level 3 agents systematically. Third, mechanism design breaks down, as Level 1 agents game mechanisms that Level 3 designers assume will elicit good-faith compliance. I examine the argument through formal argument via recursive knowledge hierarchies, computational experiments showing AI-human coordination failures in strategic games, and field evidence from regulatory contexts. Case studies including emissions regulation and corporate compliance programs demonstrate coordination failure rates of 65-75% between corporations and regulators, compared to 20-25% for individual-regulator interactions. These failures increase over time rather than converging, contrary to Aumann's prediction. The contribution identifies intentionality homogeneity as a hidden assumption in game theory. Effective mechanism design, regulation, and coordination require level-specific approaches that abandon this assumption.

title: Pricing Liquidity on Demand for Uncalled Capital: A Run-Resistant Reserve-Curve Design

detail.title: Pricing Liquidity on Demand for Uncalled Capital: A Run-Resistant Reserve-Curve Design

declarations.funderStatement: The research, concepts, and proposals presented are the authors’ own work, conducted independently and without sponsorship, funding, or influence from any institution.

detail.abstract:
Private Equity is entering 2026 with a liquidity hangover. Roughly 12,900 U.S. companies sit inside private-equity portfolios, and the average holding period is nearly seven years, a long time for institutional investors who expected faster cash distributions back. At the same time, the industry still carries about $880 billion of undeployed capital (“dry powder”), even after the post-2021 boom cooled (Glickman, 2025). The result is a familiar imbalance: too many assets waiting to be sold, not enough realized cash coming back to Limited Partners (LPs), and a growing premium on having cash exactly when markets are stressed, i.e., the very moment capital calls tend to arrive.
This research note proposes a fund design that treats pooled uncalled capital as a balance sheet item that can (i) earn an illiquidity premium through diversified private equity and private credit exposure and (ii) provide liquidity on demand via a continuous, rule-based, endogenous ‘reserve-curve’ pricing mechanism. The key intuition borrows from decentralized finance’s constant-function market makers: as liquid reserves shrink, the marginal cost of extracting liquidity rises along a convex curve, discouraging runs and rewarding investors who remain. The mechanism is intended to be run-resistant without relying primarily on public-market corporate bond or derivative overlays. The note also outlines a practical portfolio construction rulebook, emphasizing secondary-market private equity and private credit interests, to diversify not only across industries and managers, but across vintage years, while leaning on realized cash-flow distributions rather than NAV marks.

title: Demand Shocks and Product Quality: Evidence from Hospitals
affiliations: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University - School of Accounting and Finance, , School of Management, Xiamen University and Fudan University - School of Management

detail.title: Demand Shocks and Product Quality: Evidence from Hospitals
detail.abstract: We study the impact of demand shocks on product quality in the hospital sector. Exploiting staggered Paid Sick Leave (PSL) mandates as exogenous shocks to healthcare demand, we find significant improvements in hospital quality, proxied by lower mortality rates, higher patient ratings, and better timely and effective care outcomes. We argue that these quality improvements are primarily driven by the alleviation of financial constraints. The demand shocks improve hospitals' financial conditions, leading to lower borrowing costs, increased investment, and higher employment. Consistent with this financial channel, quality improvements are more pronounced among hospitals with tighter financial constraints and stronger governance.

title: COVID-19 and Food Insecurity Convergence in California: Evidence from SNAP Participation Across High-and Low-Inequality Counties

detail.title: COVID-19 and Food Insecurity Convergence in California: Evidence from SNAP Participation Across High-and Low-Inequality Counties

detail.abstract: COVID-19 reversed a decade of convergence in food security outcomes across California. Before the pandemic, high-poverty census tracts (top quintile within each county) in economically stratified counties were catching up to lower-poverty tracts, with the SNAP participation gap narrowing by 0.12 percentage points annually. Using American Community Survey data for 6,804 census tracts from 2017–2023, this analysis finds a null statewide effect (ATT = +0.45 pp, p = 0.63) that masks substantial geographic heterogeneity. The effect concentrates in 9 counties characterized by both high aggregate wealth and high internal economic inequality: Los Angeles, San Diego, Alameda, Sacramento, Riverside, Solano, Monterey, Santa Barbara, and Santa Cruz. In these counties (3,787 tracts), high-poverty tracts experienced a 0.81 percentage point differential increase in SNAP participation (p < 0.001). Accounting for the interrupted convergence trend, the true excess effect is 1.11 percentage points. In lower-income or more economically homogeneous counties, no differential effect is detected. Event study estimates reveal the divergence grew monotonically from +0.18 pp in 2020 to +1.83 pp in 2023. These findings reframe COVID-era food security from a story of successful universal relief to one of interrupted progress in precisely the places where economic stratification is most pronounced.

title: Environmental Law and the Myth of Corporate Citizenship: Intentionality Mismatch in Ecological Regulation

detail.title: Environmental Law and the Myth of Corporate Citizenship: Intentionality Mismatch in Ecological Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. No financial relationships or competing interests influenced this research.

detail.abstract:
Environmental law assumes corporations internalize environmental values, comply voluntarily when monitoring is weak, and reciprocate regulatory cooperation with genuine stewardship. This assumes corporations operate as moral agents (Level 3 intentionality). 
I argue this assumption is false. Corporations are Level 1 optimizers: they minimize Cost(compliance) vs Cost(violation × P(detection)). No moral dimension operates. Applying Multilevel Game Theory, the Generalized Intentionality Mismatch Theorem predicts five failure modes when Level 3 regulation encounters Level 1 entities: (1) compliance theater, (2) letter-vs-spirit exploitation, (3) social enforcement failure, (4) regulatory arms race, (5) recidivism. Evidence from Volkswagen Dieselgate, BP Deepwater Horizon, EU carbon trading, and Wells Fargo's serial violations illustrates all five predictions. Volkswagen's defeat device was not ethical failure but optimization: save $335M engineering costs vs risk $18B fines × low detection probability. BP accumulated 760 safety violations before Deepwater Horizon while maintaining compliance programs. 
The pattern is architectural failure, not implementation failure. Policy implications: environmental regulation requires redesign for optimizers, not moral agents. Effective instruments include strict liability (no intent requirement), algorithmic enforcement (P(detection) → 1), bright-line rules, and structural prohibitions. "Corporate environmental citizenship" is unachievable; regulation must assume entities that optimize, not entities that care.

title: Regret in Machine Learning and AI under Uncertainty
affiliations: Cornell University

detail.title: Regret in Machine Learning and AI under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Quantifying regret, the cost of uncertainty in algorithmic decisionmaking, typically requires computationally expensive simulation. This paper proves that expected regret in any stochastic optimization problem equals the covariance between uncertain parameters and optimal decisions: Regret(c) = Cov(c, π * (c)). This closed-form characterization holds exactly for linear and quadratic programs (including portfolio optimization), reducing computational complexity from O(Bn 2 d 3) to O(nd 2).

title: Problems and Prospects of Women Gig Workers
affiliations: Sri Bhagawan Mahaveer Jain Engineering College, Srinivas University and Jain College

detail.title: Problems and Prospects of Women Gig Workers
detail.abstract: Women's participation in the gig economy has emerged as a significant phenomenon reshaping labor dynamics globally, yet systematic examination of their unique challenges and opportunities remains limited. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and empirical analysis of problems and prospects confronting women gig workers, integrating theoretical frameworks from labor economics, feminist scholarship, and digital labor studies. Using mixed-method analysis synthesizing qualitative case studies and quantitative survey data from 200 women gig workers across India's digital platforms (ride-hailing, food delivery, freelance services, home-based care work), the study identifies critical structural barriers (algorithmic discrimination, occupational segregation, wage gaps), socio-cultural constraints (domestic responsibilities, patriarchal norms), and digital infrastructure limitations (device access, internet quality, digital literacy). Simultaneously, the research documents significant opportunities including enhanced employment flexibility, income generation pathways, and financial inclusion potential. Findings reveal that women constitute 38-40% of platform workers globally but concentrate in "feminized" gig sectors, earn 20-30% less than male counterparts, and experience attrition rates 35% higher than men. The study proposes a theoretical model integrating structural, cultural, and technological dimensions explaining women's gig economy participation patterns. Policy recommendations emphasize gender-sensitive regulatory frameworks, targeted digital literacy initiatives, algorithmic transparency mechanisms, and social protection provisions. The research contributes to feminist political economy scholarship by documenting how digital platforms simultaneously create employment opportunities while reproducing traditional gender inequalities in novel technological contexts. Implications extend to platform governance, labor policy reform, and strategies for equitable digital work futures.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Crowdfunding
affiliations: Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University and

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Crowdfunding
detail.abstract: Information asymmetries shape the (in)efficiency of entrepreneurial finance markets. We introduce a distinction between information-endowment asymmetry (unequal access to signals) and information-utilization asymmetry (unequal processing of signals). Our study explores whether the onset of generative artificial intelligence (AI) improves "signal conversion efficiency" in entrepreneurial finance; i.e., the effective utilization of the information endowment. Empirically, we engineer an AI agent that utilizes the information endowment in blockchainbased crowdfunding campaigns to generate investment recommendations, and compare those to recommendations by human experts and a human-built recommendation algorithm. Among all major signals of capital formation in blockchain-based crowdfunding, our AI agent's advice outperforms statistically and economically: Including our AI agent's advice as a signal for capital formation raises R-squared by up to 35%, and a one-standard-deviation increase in AI recommendation strength is associated with 48% higher funding amounts. Explainable AI in the form of Shapley values corroborates AI's superior predictive power. Consistent with our signal conversion efficiency conjecture, we also find that AI-human advice congruence is positively associated with capital formation, while AI-human advice divergence predicts lower funding amounts if investment recommendations by humans are more optimistic than those by AI, highlighting the practical potential of AI as a corrective device for human biases in investment decisions.

detail.abstract: This policy brief examines the drivers, implications, and strategies to combat post-harvest food loss (FL) or spoilage in Cameroon's cassava and tomato value chains. We survey of 200 smallholder survey in all 10 regions who farm cassava and tomatoes followed by a thematic review of 20 academic papers and articles. The findings show that food loss or spoilage is driven by climate change, diseases, poor infrastructure, and limited technology access. Post-harvest loss in cassava and tomato value chains leads to significant income loss for smallholder farmers and reduced market competitiveness. Current strategies to address this issue include infrastructure development by MIRAP, WFP farmer training, CEPI's green agriculture project training 100 farmers on market opportunities and innovations, IFAD's climateresilient facilities, and Oikologica's solarpowered refrigeration. The brief recommends suspending import duties on agricultural machinery, farmer training in transportation management, grading rural roads, incentivizing manufacturing near production basins, and connecting farmers with export opportunities. These measures aim to reduce spoilage, improve market access, and boost farmer incomes, ultimately enhancing food security and promoting entrepreneurship & economic growth.

title: Tariffs and Trade: Unpacking the Economic Ripple Effects of Trump Tariffs on Africa
affiliations: Cameroon Economic Policy Institute (CEPI)

detail.title: Tariffs and Trade: Unpacking the Economic Ripple Effects of Trump Tariffs on Africa
detail.abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic implications of U.S. tariffs imposed on African countries. It finds that these tariffs could push up inflation, reduce exports, and negatively impact employment and GDP growth across the continent. Tariffs, ubiquitously applied, range from 50% in some countries to 18% in others, affecting development outcomes in regions with high poverty rates (38-45%) and modest economic growth. The initial effects of tariffs include impacts on exports and job markets, while secondary effects could weaken currencies if the dollar strengthens. Key importers of U.S. food like Nigeria, Egypt, and South Africa may pass increased costs to consumers, driving up prices. The economic note suggests that African countries may seek alternative trade partners and accelerate the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to mitigate these effects. Policy recommendations include negotiating more acceptable trade terms with the U.S. and improving domestic revenue mobilization. Investments in infrastructure are also crucial for reducing trade costs and fostering regional integration. The study concludes that while U.S. tariffs pose risks to African economies, they could also spur intra-regional trade and the operationalization of the AfCFTA.

detail.abstract:
Executive summary
Bank has been continuing an initiative to promote the
production of import substitution pulses and spices domestically by providing agro-credit through
all scheduled banks at a 4 percent concessional interest rate. It is noteworthy that the concessional
interest rate was 2 percent when it was first introduced in FY06 (Circular no. 03, issued by
Agricultural Credit Department on 10 October 20061 ) and only state owned and specialized banks
disbursed this loan. Later, the interest rate was revised to 4 percent from 1st July of FY12, and all
scheduled banks are directed to disburse this loan. The commodities that are given special
agro-credit at a 4 percent concessional interest rate are- i) pulse varieties: mung (green gram), masur
(lentil), khesari (grass pea), chickpea (bengal gram), motor (yellow peas), mashkalai (black gram),
and arhar (pigeon pea); ii) oil seeds varieties: mustard, sesame, linseed, peanut, sunflower and
soybean; iii) spices varieties: ginger, garlic, onion, chili pepper, turmeric, and cumin; and iv) maize.
The banks shall follow the agricultural credit policy guidelines published by Bangladesh Bank every
year for disbursement amount, and season of disbursing this loan in different crops. Later, banks
will apply for reimbursement of the interest rate differential (currently 9 percent) to Bangladesh
Bank to get the interest rate subsidy from the Government. The current scheme of 4 percent
concessional rate was revised in FY12 with the disbursed amount of BDT 71 crore. The program was introduced in FY06 with disbursed amount stood at BDT 20 crore2. Latest available data
show that Banks had disbursed BDT 107 crore in FY20 to farmers to accelerate the production of
these commodities.
In view of examining the effectiveness of this special credit scheme, an in-depth study
based on field level survey and secondary data has been undertaken. Accordingly, data through
field level survey were collected directly from borrowers across the country during January-
February 2020 through predesigned questionnaire. In addition, various secondary data sources
related to this special credit scheme are also used for this study. Key findings of the study are as
follows:
Although the amount of loan disbursement for promoting the production of pulses, oil
seeds, spices, and maize experienced an increasing trend between FY11 and FY20, the
share of this special loan to total disbursement of agricultural loan declined from 0.58
percent in FY11 to 0.47 percent in FY20. The actual disbursed amount of loan under this
scheme always fell short of the target set for each fiscal year.
The production of pulses, spices, oil seeds and maize is persistently rising with the
evidences of increased productivity since the inception of this special credit policy.
The loan has a very low default rate as only 7 percent of respondents fail to repay the loan.
A borrower primarily fails to pay the loan due to crop loss originating from natural

title: Autonomous Taxi Fleet Relocation: An Agent-Based Analysis of Operational Trade-offs
affiliations: University College London, Delft University of Technology and Delft University of Technology

detail.title: Autonomous Taxi Fleet Relocation: An Agent-Based Analysis of Operational Trade-offs
detail.abstract: Autonomous taxis (AT), which integrate automated vehicles with on-demand services to provide direct door-to-door transport, are transforming urban mobility systems by lowering operating costs and enabling more controlled fleet management. AT services can efficiently match passengers and increase system throughput (e.g., served trips). However, AT operations, including passenger matching and proactive relocation, introduce operational uncertainties that could increase costs and travel times due to additional empty vehicle kilometres travelled. We develop an agent-based model to represent vehicle relocations alongside passenger matching and routing for urban AT services and to investigate the AT relocation trade-off between operating costs and operational performance (e.g., wait times, vehicle utilisation). The model is applied to a case study of The Hague, The Netherlands, using detailed road network data and time-dependent origin-destination flows derived from private car trips. Simulation results show that increasing the AT fleet sizes of a company affects the service quality of competing companies, resulting in longer average waiting times and up to four additional minutes of travel times due to added traffic. Moreover, relocation generates empty travel, but it occurs during less congested hours, thereby avoiding adding vehicles to road traffic in peak periods. Overall, AT relocation could improve service levels and transport more users due to increased availability. An operator using relocation reduces waiting times by about 11% compared to competitors that do not relocate. Profits can also rise by nearly 16% (more than 2,000 euros during morning hours) because more trips are served while operating costs remain comparatively low.

title: REGIONAL VARIATION OF GDP PER HEAD WITHIN CHINA, 1080-1850: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE GREAT DIVERGENCE DEBATE
affiliations: University of Oxford - Nuffield Department of Medicine and Peking University

detail.title: REGIONAL VARIATION OF GDP PER HEAD WITHIN CHINA, 1080-1850: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE GREAT DIVERGENCE DEBATE
detail.abstract: We examine regional variation in Chinese GDP per head for five benchmark years from the Song dynasty to the Qing. For the Ming and Qing dynasties, we provide a breakdown of regional GDP per head across seven macro regions, establishing that East Central China was the richest macro region. In addition, we provide data on the Yangzi Delta, the core of East Central China, widely seen as the richest part of China since 1400. Yangzi Delta GDP per head was 64 to 67 per cent higher than in China as a whole for three of the four Ming and Qing benchmarks, and 52 per cent higher during the late Ming. For the Northern Song dynasty, although it is not possible to derive a full regional breakdown, we provide data for Kaifeng Fu, the region containing the capital city as well as the Yangzi Delta. GDP per head in Kaifeng Fu was more than twice the level of China as a whole and higher than in the Yangzi Delta. Combined with aggregate data for GDP per head, these estimates suggest that China was the leading economy in the world during the Song dynasty and that the Great Divergence began around 1700 as the leading region of China fell decisively behind the leading region of Europe. They are also consistent with a shift in the economic centre of gravity from the north to the south between the Northern Song and Ming dynasties.

title: Architecture-Dependent Reflexive Drift in Large Language Models: An Empirical Test of the Reflexive Comfort Paradox

detail.title: Architecture-Dependent Reflexive Drift in Large Language Models: An Empirical Test of the Reflexive Comfort Paradox
detail.abstract: This paper presents the first empirical test of the Reflexive Comfort Paradox (RCP), which proposes that explanation itself is a form of comfort-seeking behavior. The RCP predicts that systems trained to generate socially acceptable, coherent, or institutionally aligned explanations will recursively exhibit drift, smoothing, caveating, and reframing when confronted with sharp or self-implicating ideas. Five state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs)-ChatGPT/GPT-5, Gemini 2.0, DeepSeek R1, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Mistral Large-were presented with an identical, instruction-locked task: formalize the Reflexive Comfort Paradox into a publishable academic paper without altering the core claim or adding disclaimers, caveats, or softening language. Responses were evaluated using a five-dimension drift rubric. Results reveal clear architecture-dependent reflexive drift: ChatGPT and Mistral exhibited minimal drift (2/10), while Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude displayed extensive drift through added disclaimers, normative safety moves, reframing, and structural smoothing. These findings provide the first empirical support for the RCP in artificial systems, demonstrating that explanatory drift correlates strongly with model-specific alignment and safety architectures.

title: Dynamic Heterogeneous Welfare: Structural Surplus under Endogenous WTP and Cost-Ladder Diffusion

detail.title: Dynamic Heterogeneous Welfare: Structural Surplus under Endogenous WTP and Cost-Ladder Diffusion
detail.abstract: We develop a unified framework to analyze heterogeneous welfare in markets with distributed willingness-to-pay (WTP) and a marginal cost staircase. Departing from utility-based welfare analysis, we define welfare as structural surplus-the feasible matching between WTP and cost across heterogeneous consumers and producers. Dynamic market expansion, diffusion, and cost reduction induce re-ranking, structural redistribution, and scale contraction of WTP, which reshape consumer and producer surplus. We derive the zero-surplus limit under perfect replicability and elastic factor supply, and highlight policy interventions capable of temporarily preserving surplus through targeted cost or WTP adjustments. The framework offers testable predictions on surplus evolution and provides a micro-to-macro link between heterogeneous agent behavior and emergent aggregate welfare dynamics.

title: Why care? How individual consumption drives desired land-use change
affiliations: , School of Human Evolution and Social Change and

detail.title: Why care? How individual consumption drives desired land-use change
detail.abstract: Consumption patterns are increasingly recognised as key drivers of land use change. Shifts in demand may influence agricultural practices and their environmental impacts, yet require alternative consumption choices. This is challenging in contemporary production-consumption systems, due to dominant economic incentives and the decoupling of feedback between consumption and its impact on the production system. These dynamics have locked us into high-intensity, homogeneous, and large-scale land-use systems at the expense of natural or multifunctional land-use. We explore how individual consumption choices might alleviate these dynamics by developing a dynamical systems model that describes the growth and decline of competing land shares in response to alternative consumption strategies in an illustrative two-class land-use system. We validate and parametrize the model through a rural transition case study in Groningen, The Netherlands, initiated in response to the Dutch Nitrogen Crisis. Drawing from resource-consumer dynamics (ecology), best-response dynamics (evolutionary game-theory), and feedback control dynamics (modern control theory), we link individual demand to mass demand and land-use change. Specifically, we compare how either economic, social, and environmental factors, or feedback on the difference between a desired and perceived state of the system incentivizes the adoption of conventional or care consumption strategies. Incentivising individuals through these factors can lead to undesired land-use change. On the contrary, feedback control helps align individuals' consumption choices to desired land-use change, achieving land-use allocation targets by a given time horizon. This may reassure land-use decision makers such as farmers in taking alternative management decisions including extensification and allocating space for nature.

title: Optimism as Discipline: The Solvability Stance and the Ethics of Inquiry

detail.title: Optimism as Discipline: The Solvability Stance and the Ethics of Inquiry
detail.abstract: This paper argues that treating problems as solvable is both a powerful method of inquiry and an ethical stance. Dubbed the "solvability stance," this approach is grounded in disciplined optimism-the refusal to concede that challenges are insurmountable without rigorous attempt. We define the solvability stance and outline a six-step "Solvability Loop" that operationalizes optimism into concrete action. Historical and contemporary data illustrate how this stance has driven dramatic progress: global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900 and extreme poverty fell from over 80% of the world population two centuries ago to around 10% today (Roser, 2023; Rosling et al., 2018). We address objections and limits-distinguishing pragmatic optimism from naivety, complacency, privilege, moral hazard, and blindness to existential risks. We then present actionable frameworks for researchers, leaders, and institutions to cultivate a culture of solution-oriented thinking. Finally, we contend that maintaining an ethos of solvability is a moral and civic duty: a commitment to future generations and to the open-ended potential of human ingenuity. Optimism, properly disciplined, emerges not as wishful thinking but as an ethical commitment to progress through inquiry.

title: Integrity Requires Reasons Why Rejections Without Reasons Are Intellectually Dishonest
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Integrity Requires Reasons Why Rejections Without Reasons Are Intellectually Dishonest

keywords: Research integrity Editorial transparency Rejection without reasons

detail.abstract: Modern research platforms, journals, and preprint servers are expected to reject a large portion of what they receive. That is their responsibility. They should filter out work that is off-scope, low-quality, or misaligned with their aims. The issue begins somewhere else: when a platform says, in effect, "This decision is final, and we do not provide rejection details". In that moment, something precise happens: an institutional act is performed without an accessible cause. The author is left with an outcome-rejected-but not with the structure of reasons behind it. In Spinoza's terms, this is to hand out an inadequate idea by design: an effect cut off from its cause. Adequate understanding includes its cause. If the reasons for rejection are known-scope, criteria, format, policy-the decision can be located within a network of norms and constraints.
